title: Two Sum
statement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the **indices of two different elements** whose values add up to `target`.

Each input has at least one valid pair. Any valid pair is accepted, in either order.
constraints: At least one valid answer exists.

gens.name: Large input (n = 100,000)
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    n = 100000
    nums = rng.sample(range(-10**9, 10**9), n)
    i, j = n - 2, n - 1
    return [nums, nums[i] + nums[j]]

hints: A brute force checks every pair: O(n²). Which inner loop can you remove?
For each x you need target − x. Can you look that up in O(1)?
Check the map before inserting x, so an element is never paired with itself.
approach:
**Hash map of values seen so far.** Walk the array once. For each `x` at index `i`, the partner you need is `target − x`. If it is already in the map, return both indices; otherwise record `x ↦ i`.

Checking before inserting guarantees the two indices differ.
complexity: O(n) time · O(n) space
followups: What if the array is sorted? (Two pointers, O(1) space.)
What if the numbers arrive as a stream and you must answer 'is there a pair for target T?' many times?
Return every pair that sums to the target, without duplicates.

title: Merge Sorted Array
statement:
`nums1` has length `m + n`: its first `m` values are sorted and the last `n` slots are placeholders (0). `nums2` holds `n` sorted values.

Merge `nums2` into `nums1` **in place** so that `nums1` is sorted. Do not return anything — the judge reads `nums1` after your method runs.
hints: Filling from the front would overwrite values of nums1 you still need.
The free space is at the end — fill nums1 from the back, largest first.
Stop when nums2 is exhausted; whatever remains of nums1 is already in place.
approach: Merge **from the back**. Pointers `i` (end of the real values of `nums1`), `j` (end of `nums2`) and `k` (last slot). Place the larger of `nums1[i]` and `nums2[j]` at `k` and step back. Writes never overtake unread values because there are exactly `n` free slots ahead of `i`.
complexity: O(m + n) time · O(1) space
followups: Merge k sorted arrays.
What if nums1 had no spare space?
Merge two sorted linked lists (#21).

title: Logger Rate Limiter
pattern: Hash map of next allowed time
statement:
Design a logger that receives a stream of messages with timestamps (in seconds, non-decreasing). Each **unique message** may be printed at most once every 10 seconds: if `message` is printed at time `t`, the same message is suppressed until time `t + 10`.

* `Logger()` initialises the logger.
* `shouldPrintMessage(timestamp, message)` returns `true` if the message should be printed now (and records that it was), otherwise `false`.
hints: For each message you only need to know when it may next be printed.
Store message → timestamp + 10 when it is printed.
Follow-up: memory grows with every distinct message. How would you clean up old entries?
approach:
Keep a hash map `message → earliest time it may print again`. A call prints (and updates the map) if `timestamp ≥ next_ok[message]`.

Memory grows with distinct messages; a common follow-up keeps a queue of the last 10 seconds of printed messages and evicts expired ones, bounding memory by the recent traffic.
complexity: O(1) average per call · O(distinct messages) space
followups: Bound memory to messages seen in the last 10 seconds.
Allow at most N prints per window (sliding-window rate limiter).
Timestamps can arrive out of order by up to 2 seconds.
Many servers share one limiter — what changes?

title: Valid Word Abbreviation
statement:
A string can be abbreviated by replacing any number of **non-adjacent, non-empty** substrings with their lengths. Lengths must not have leading zeros.

For example `"substitution"` can be written `"s10n"`, `"sub4u4"` or `"12"`, but not `"s010n"` (leading zero) or `"s0ubstitution"` (empty replacement).

Given `word` and `abbr`, return `true` if `abbr` is a valid abbreviation of `word`.
constraints: word is lowercase letters; abbr is lowercase letters and digits.

examples.explanation: 'a' + 2 letters lands on 'l', not 'e'.

hints: Walk both strings with two pointers.
When you meet a digit in abbr, read the whole number, then jump the word pointer forward by that many.
Reject a number that starts with '0'. At the end, both pointers must be exactly at the ends.
approach: Two pointers: `i` over `word`, `j` over `abbr`. Letters must match one-for-one. A run of digits is parsed into a number `k` (rejecting a leading `0`) and moves `i` forward by `k`. The abbreviation is valid only if both pointers finish exactly at the end of their strings.
complexity: O(len(abbr)) time · O(1) space
followups: What if uppercase letters in abbr may match any letter (wildcards)?
Generate every valid abbreviation of a word (Generalized Abbreviation, #320).
Check one abbreviation against a dictionary of words efficiently.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: The **diameter** of a binary tree is the number of **edges** on the longest path between any two nodes. The path does not have to pass through the root. Return the diameter.
starter:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        pass

gens.name: Tree with 10,000 nodes
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [rand_tree(rng, 10000, distinct=False)]

hints: The longest path through a node = height(left) + height(right).
Compute heights bottom-up (postorder) and update a global best on the way.
Calling a separate height() for every node is O(n²) on a skewed tree.
approach: One **postorder** pass returns each subtree's height (in nodes). At each node, `height(left) + height(right)` is the longest path bending there; keep the maximum. Each node is processed once.
complexity: O(n) time · O(h) space
followups: Diameter of an n-ary tree (#1522).
Diameter of a general tree / graph — two BFS passes.
Return the path, not just its length.

title: Valid Palindrome II
statement: Given a string `s`, return `true` if it can become a palindrome after deleting **at most one** character.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Delete 'c' (or 'b').

gens.name: Long string with one extra character
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    half = "".join(rng.choice("ab") for _ in range(50000))
    s = half + half[::-1]
    k = 70000
    return [s[:k] + "z" + s[k:]]

hints: Compare characters from both ends with two pointers.
At the first mismatch you have exactly two choices: skip the left character or skip the right one.
After that one skip, the rest must be a plain palindrome — no more skips allowed.
approach:
Move two pointers inwards while characters match. At the **first mismatch** `s[i] ≠ s[j]`, the deleted character must be one of these two, so check whether `s[i+1..j]` or `s[i..j−1]` is a palindrome.

Trying every deletion is O(n²); this needs at most two extra linear scans.
complexity: O(n) time · O(1) space
followups: Allow up to k deletions (Valid Palindrome III — becomes DP on the longest palindromic subsequence).
Return the index to delete instead of true / false.
Ignore non-alphanumeric characters and case, as in Valid Palindrome (#125).

title: Range Sum of BST
statement: Given the root of a **binary search tree** and a range `[low, high]`, return the sum of all node values inside the range (inclusive). Use the BST property to skip subtrees that cannot contribute.
starter:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def rangeSumBST(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], low: int, high: int) -> int:
        pass

gens.name: BST with 20,000 nodes
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [rand_tree(rng, 20000, bst=True), 1000, 3000]

hints: A plain traversal adding values in range already works in O(n).
If node.val < low, nothing in its left subtree can be in range — skip it.
Symmetrically, if node.val > high, skip the right subtree.
approach: DFS, adding values within `[low, high]`, but only descend left when `node.val > low` and right when `node.val < high`. The pruning keeps the work proportional to the nodes in (and bordering) the range.
complexity: O(n) worst case, O(h + k) with pruning (k nodes in range) · O(h) space
followups: Many range queries on a static BST — precompute prefix sums over the inorder sequence.
Count the nodes in range instead.
The tree is not a BST — what changes?

title: Add Two Numbers
statement:
Two non-negative integers are stored as linked lists with their digits in **reverse order** (the head is the ones digit). Return their sum as a linked list in the same format.

Lists are shown as arrays: `[2,4,3]` is 2 → 4 → 3, i.e. the number 342.
constraints: No leading zeros except the number 0 itself.
starter:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: Optional[ListNode], l2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        pass
reference:
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1, l2):
        dummy = tail = ListNode()
        carry = 0
        while l1 or l2 or carry:
            s = carry + (l1.val if l1 else 0) + (l2.val if l2 else 0)
            carry, digit = divmod(s, 10)
            tail.next = ListNode(digit)
            tail = tail.next
            l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
            l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
        return dummy.next
hints: Add digit by digit like on paper — the lists are already least-significant first.
Carry the overflow into the next position.
A dummy head node avoids special-casing the first digit. Keep going while either list or the carry remains.
approach: Walk both lists together, adding the two digits plus `carry`; write `sum % 10` into a new node and carry `sum // 10`. Continue while either list has nodes **or** a carry remains (that is what produces the extra leading 1 in 999 + 1). A dummy head keeps the code uniform.
complexity: O(max(m, n)) time · O(1) extra space (output excluded)
followups: Digits stored most-significant first (#445) — use stacks or reverse.
Subtract or multiply instead of add.
Why does converting to an integer fail in Java or C++ for 100-digit numbers?

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest **substring** (contiguous) that contains no repeated characters.
constraints: s may contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces.

examples.explanation: 'abc'
'wke'. Note 'pwke' is a subsequence, not a substring.

gens.name: Long string, large alphabet

hints: Keep a window [left, right] that never contains a repeat.
When s[right] is already inside the window, move left just past its previous position.
Store the last index of each character so the jump is O(1).
approach:
**Variable-size sliding window.** Extend `right` one step at a time. If the new character was last seen at an index ≥ `left`, it is inside the window, so jump `left` to one past that index. The window is always repeat-free; track the largest width.

Each index enters and leaves the window at most once.
complexity: O(n) time · O(min(n, alphabet)) space
followups: At most k distinct characters (#340).
At most two repeats of any character.
Return the substring itself, and all substrings of maximal length.

title: Generate Parentheses
statement: Return **all** combinations of `n` pairs of well-formed parentheses, in any order.
hints: Build the string one character at a time.
You may add '(' while fewer than n are open; you may add ')' only while it would close something.
Those two rules prune every invalid prefix, so every leaf is a valid answer.
approach: **Backtracking with two counters.** Extend the current string with `'('` if `open < n`, and with `')'` if `close < open`. When the length reaches `2n`, record it. Because invalid prefixes are never created, the work is proportional to the output (the n-th Catalan number).
complexity: O(4ⁿ / √n) time and space (Catalan number of results)
followups: Only count them (Catalan numbers, DP).
Generate them in lexicographic order.
Three bracket types with correct nesting.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
pattern: Binary search — find the sorted half
statement:
A sorted array of **distinct** integers was rotated at an unknown pivot (for example `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` → `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`). Return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it is absent.

Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.
hints: At any mid, at least one half — [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] — is sorted.
Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half's range.
If it does, search that half; otherwise search the other half.
approach: Ordinary binary search plus one question per step: **which half is sorted?** If `nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid]`, the left half is sorted and you can test `nums[lo] ≤ target < nums[mid]` directly; otherwise the right half is sorted. Discard the half that cannot contain the target.
complexity: O(log n) time · O(1) space
followups: Duplicates allowed (#81) — what is the worst case now?
Find the rotation point / minimum (#153).
Return the first and last index of the target in a rotated array with duplicates.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Group the strings in `strs` that are anagrams of one another. Return the groups in any order; the strings inside a group may also be in any order.

gens.name: 10,000 strings

hints: Two words are anagrams exactly when their letters, sorted, are equal.
Use that sorted form as a dictionary key.
A 26-length count tuple also works as a key and avoids the sort.
approach: Map every string to a **canonical key** shared by all its anagrams — its sorted letters (or a tuple of 26 letter counts) — and append it to the list for that key. The dictionary's values are the groups.
complexity: O(n · k log k) time with sorting, O(n · k) with counts · O(n · k) space
followups: Strings are very long — which key is cheaper?
Group strings that are rotations / shifts of each other (#249).

title: Pow(x, n)
statement:
Compute `x` raised to the integer power `n`, without using `**` or `pow()`.

Results are compared with a relative tolerance of 10⁻⁵.
hints: Multiplying n times is far too slow when n is about two billion.
x^n = (x^(n/2))² when n is even, and x · x^(n−1) when n is odd.
For negative n, compute (1/x)^(−n).
approach: **Exponentiation by squaring.** Look at the bits of `n`: square `x` at every step, and multiply it into the result when the current bit is 1. That needs about log₂n multiplications. Handle a negative exponent by inverting `x` first (in Python `-n` cannot overflow; in Java / C++ use a 64-bit copy of `n`).
complexity: O(log |n|) time · O(1) space (iterative)
followups: Compute (xⁿ) mod m for huge n (modular exponentiation).
Raise a 2×2 matrix to the n-th power to get Fibonacci in O(log n).
Write the recursive version — what is its space complexity?

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Return all elements of the `m × n` matrix in **spiral order**: along the top row left to right, down the right column, along the bottom row right to left, up the left column, then continue inwards.
hints: Keep four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
Walk one side, then move that boundary inwards.
Single remaining rows or columns are where off-by-one bugs live — guard the bottom and left walks.
approach: Maintain `top, bottom, left, right`. Each lap walks the top row, the right column, the bottom row (only if `top < bottom`) and the left column (only if `left < right`), then shrinks all four boundaries. The two guards stop a single leftover row or column from being read twice.
complexity: O(m · n) time · O(1) extra space
followups: Generate an n × n spiral matrix (#59).
Spiral from the centre outwards.
Rotate the matrix 90° in place (#48).

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Merge all overlapping intervals `[start, end]` and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover exactly the same ranges. Intervals that touch (`[1,4]` and `[4,5]`) overlap.

gens.name: 10,000 intervals

hints: Sort by start time first.
Then every interval can only overlap the last merged one.
Overlap test after sorting: start ≤ last end. Extend the end with max().
approach: **Sort by start, then sweep.** After sorting, an interval either overlaps the last interval in the output (`start ≤ last.end`) — extend it with `max` — or starts a new one.
complexity: O(n log n) time · O(n) space
followups: Insert one new interval into an already merged list (#57) in O(n).
Intervals arrive as a stream (#352).
Return the total length covered.

title: Simplify Path
constraints: path is an absolute path made of letters, digits, '.', '/' and '_'.
hints: Split on '/' and handle each piece.
Empty pieces and '.' do nothing; '..' undoes the last directory if there is one.
A stack of directory names holds exactly the canonical path.
approach: Split the path on `/`. Ignore empty pieces and `.`; on `..` pop the stack if it is not empty; push anything else. Join the stack with `/` and prefix a single `/`.
complexity: O(n) time · O(n) space
followups: Support a current working directory and relative paths (cd command simulation).
Resolve symbolic links given as a mapping.
Return the result as a list of components for a file-system tree lookup.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
pattern: Hash set, start only at sequence heads
statement:
Given an unsorted array `nums`, return the length of the longest run of **consecutive integers** (x, x+1, x+2, …) that all appear in `nums`. Order in the array does not matter.

Aim for O(n) time.

gens.name: One long run of 100,000
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    a = list(range(-50000, 50000)); rng.shuffle(a); return [a]

hints: Sorting gives O(n log n). For O(n), put everything in a set.
Only start counting from x if x − 1 is not in the set — x is the head of a run.
Each number is then visited at most twice.
approach: Put the numbers in a hash set. A value `x` starts a run only if `x − 1` is absent; from each such head, walk `x+1, x+2, …` while present. Because inner walks only start at heads, every number is examined a constant number of times.
complexity: O(n) time · O(n) space
followups: Numbers arrive as a stream; report the longest run after each insertion (Union-Find).
Return the run itself.
Why is the brute force (start a walk from every x) O(n²)?

title: Word Break
statement: Return `true` if `s` can be split into a sequence of one or more words from `wordDict`. A dictionary word may be used any number of times.
constraints: All words are distinct and lowercase.

examples.explanation: Words may be reused.

hints: Plain recursion re-solves the same suffix many times — 'aaaa…ab' takes exponential time.
Let ok[i] mean 'the first i characters can be segmented'.
ok[i] is true if some word w ends at i and ok[i − len(w)] is true.
approach: `ok[i]` = can `s[:i]` be segmented? `ok[0] = True`. For each `i`, try each dictionary word length `L`: if `ok[i − L]` and `s[i−L:i]` is a word, then `ok[i] = True`. The answer is `ok[n]`. Top-down recursion with `@lru_cache` on the start index is the same idea.
complexity: O(n · m · L) time (m distinct word lengths, L for slicing) · O(n) space
followups: Return every possible sentence (#140).
The dictionary is huge — store it in a trie and walk forward from each ok position.
Minimum number of words in a segmentation.

title: LRU Cache
statement:
Design a **least-recently-used cache** with a fixed capacity.

* `LRUCache(capacity)` creates the cache.
* `get(key)` returns the value for `key`, or `-1` if it is absent. A successful `get` counts as a use.
* `put(key, value)` inserts or updates `key`. If this pushes the cache over capacity, evict the least recently used key first.

Both `get` and `put` must run in **O(1)** average time.

examples.explanation: put(3,3) evicts key 2 (key 1 was just used); put(4,4) evicts key 1.

gens.name: 100,000 operations, capacity 3,000

hints: A hash map gives O(1) lookup, but not 'which key is least recently used'.
A doubly linked list ordered by recency can move a node to the front and drop the tail in O(1).
Combine them: the map stores key → list node. (In Python, OrderedDict does exactly this.)
approach:
Pair a **hash map** (key → node) with a **doubly linked list** ordered by recency. `get` looks the node up and moves it to the most-recent end; `put` updates or inserts at that end and, when over capacity, removes the node at the least-recent end and deletes its key from the map. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove all edge cases.

Python's `OrderedDict` (`move_to_end`, `popitem(last=False)`) is the same structure; interviewers often ask you to build the linked list yourself.
complexity: O(1) average per operation · O(capacity) space
followups: Implement the doubly linked list yourself, without OrderedDict.
LFU cache (#460).
Make it thread-safe.
Add a time-to-live per entry.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
pattern: Binary search against the right end
statement: A sorted array of **distinct** integers has been rotated between 1 and n times. Return its minimum element in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: Rotated n times — back to sorted.

hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi], not nums[lo].
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop (and the minimum) is strictly to the right of mid.
Otherwise mid..hi is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left — keep mid.
approach: Binary search for the **rotation point**. If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the array drops somewhere after `mid`, so `lo = mid + 1`. Otherwise `[mid, hi]` is sorted and the minimum is at or before `mid`, so `hi = mid`. When `lo == hi` it points at the minimum.
complexity: O(log n) time · O(1) space
followups: Duplicates allowed (#154) — worst case becomes O(n). Why?
Return the number of rotations.
Use the rotation point to search for a target (#33).

title: Find Peak Element
statement:
A **peak** is an element strictly greater than its neighbours. Imagine `nums[-1] = nums[n] = −∞`. Neighbouring elements are never equal.

Return the index of **any** peak. Aim for O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: Index 1 is also a peak and is accepted.

gens.name: Large input (n = 100,000)
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    a = list(range(100000))
    a[-1] = -1
    return [a]

hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1].
If the right neighbour is larger you are walking uphill — a peak must exist to the right.
Otherwise a peak exists at mid or to its left. Halve the range each time.
approach: **Binary search on the slope.** If `nums[mid] < nums[mid+1]`, the sequence rises to the right and, because `nums[n] = −∞`, must come down again — so a peak lies in `(mid, hi]`. Otherwise one lies in `[lo, mid]`. The range always contains a peak and shrinks by half each step.
complexity: O(log n) time · O(1) space
followups: Find a peak in a 2D grid (#1901).
Why does the argument fail if neighbours can be equal?
Return all peaks — what is the best possible time then?

title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
statement:
Implement an iterator over a BST that returns values in ascending order (an inorder traversal).

* `BSTIterator(root)` initialises it.
* `next()` returns the next smallest value.
* `hasNext()` returns `true` if values remain.

Aim for O(1) average time per call and O(h) memory, where h is the tree height.
constraints: next() is only called when hasNext() is true.

gens.name: BST with 50,000 nodes

hints: Storing the full inorder list works but uses O(n) memory.
Iterative inorder keeps a stack of the left spine — pause it between calls.
next(): pop a node, then push the left spine of its right child. Each node is pushed and popped once.
approach: **Paused iterative inorder.** The stack always holds the path of unvisited ancestors. Start by pushing the left spine of the root. `next()` pops the smallest node and pushes the left spine of its right subtree. Every node is pushed and popped exactly once, so calls are O(1) amortised, and the stack never exceeds the tree height.
complexity: O(1) amortised per call · O(h) space
followups: Add a prev() / hasPrev() (#1586).
Two iterators to solve Two Sum IV on a BST in O(h) space.
Iterate in descending order.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
pattern: BFS by level (last node) / DFS right-first
statement: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom — the **rightmost node of each level**.
starter:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def rightSideView(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
        pass

gens.name: Tree with 100,000 nodes
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [rand_tree(rng, 100000, -100, 100, distinct=False)]

hints: Process the tree level by level.
The last node of each level is visible from the right.
Alternatively, DFS visiting the right child first; the first node reached at each depth is visible.
approach: **Level-order traversal**: for each level, record its last node. Equivalent DFS: visit right before left and record a node the first time its depth is reached.
complexity: O(n) time · O(w) space (w = widest level)
followups: Left side view.
Return the boundary of the tree (#545).
View from the top or bottom — needs column indices (see #314).

title: Number of Islands
statement: `grid` is a map of `"1"` (land) and `"0"` (water). An **island** is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically. Return the number of islands. Everything outside the grid is water.

gens.name: 300 × 300 grid
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [[[("1" if rng.random() < 0.45 else "0") for _ in range(300)] for _ in range(300)]]

hints: Every unvisited land cell you meet starts a new island.
From it, flood-fill (BFS or DFS) to mark the entire island as visited.
The number of flood fills you start is the answer.
approach:
Scan every cell. When an unvisited `"1"` is found, increment the count and **flood fill** its island with BFS or DFS, marking cells visited (or overwriting them with `"0"` if mutating the input is acceptable — say so in an interview).

Recursive DFS can hit Python's recursion limit on a 300 × 300 snake-shaped island; BFS or an explicit stack avoids that.
complexity: O(R · C) time · O(R · C) space worst case
followups: Count distinct island shapes (#694).
Cells turn into land one at a time; report the count after each (#305, Union-Find).
Max area of an island (#695).
The grid is too large for memory — process it row by row.

title: Course Schedule
statement:
There are `numCourses` courses labelled `0 … numCourses − 1`. Each pair `[a, b]` in `prerequisites` means course `b` must be taken before course `a`.

Return `true` if it is possible to finish every course.

examples.explanation: Each course needs the other first — a cycle.

gens.name: 2,000 courses, 5,000 prerequisites
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    n = 2000

Scan once, keeping the current `num` and the **previous operator** `op`. When an operator (or the end) arrives, apply `op` to `num`:

approach: Two pointers. For the current pair, the intersection is `[max(a₀, b₀), min(a₁, b₁)]` if non-empty. Then drop whichever interval **ends first**: every later interval in the other list starts after the current one, so it cannot meet the finished interval again.
complexity: O(m + n) time · O(1) extra space
followups: Union of the two lists instead.
k lists at once (use a heap).
Free time common to all employees (#759).

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
statement: `nums` contains only 0s and 1s. You may flip **at most `k`** zeros to ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive 1s you can obtain.

gens.name: n = 100,000
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [[1 if rng.random() < 0.97 else 0 for _ in range(100000)], 2000]

hints: Rephrase: the longest window containing at most k zeros.
Grow the window to the right, counting zeros.
When the count exceeds k, shrink from the left until it is back to k.
approach: **Sliding window with a zero budget.** Expand `right`; when the window holds more than `k` zeros, advance `left` until it holds `k`. The window then always describes a run achievable with ≤ k flips; track its maximum width. Each index enters and leaves once.
complexity: O(n) time · O(1) space
followups: k = 1 with a stream of bits (#487) — store only the last zero's position.
Longest repeating character replacement (#424).
Return the positions to flip.

title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
statement: In an `n × n` grid of 0s (open) and 1s (blocked), find the length of the shortest **clear path** from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. Moves go to any of the **8** neighbouring cells. The length counts cells visited, including both ends. Return `-1` if there is no such path.

gens.name: 100 × 100 grid
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    g = [[1 if rng.random() < 0.25 else 0 for _ in range(100)] for _ in range(100)]
    g[0][0] = g[99][99] = 0
    return [g]

hints: Every move costs the same, so BFS gives the shortest path.
Neighbours are the 8 surrounding cells.
Check the start and end cells first; mark cells visited when you enqueue them.
approach:
Plain **BFS** from `(0, 0)` over open cells with 8-directional moves, storing the path length (in cells) for each visited cell. The first time the bottom-right cell is dequeued, its distance is the answer. Blocked start or end → −1.

A* with the Chebyshev distance as heuristic is a common follow-up optimisation.
complexity: O(n²) time and space
followups: Use A* — what heuristic is admissible with diagonal moves?
Return the path itself.
Allow removing up to k obstacles (#1293).

title: Car Pooling
statement:
A car drives only east and has `capacity` empty seats. `trips[i] = [numPassengers, from, to]`: that many passengers board at kilometre `from` and leave at kilometre `to`.

Return `true` if every trip can be completed without ever exceeding the capacity.
hints: Only the kilometres where someone boards or leaves matter.
Turn each trip into two events: +n at `from`, −n at `to`.
Sort the events and keep a running load; at equal positions, process drop-offs first.
approach:
**Sweep line.** Each trip adds `+n` at `from` and `−n` at `to`. Sort the events by position — tuples sort `(km, −n)` before `(km, +n)`, so passengers leave before new ones board at the same stop — and keep a running total; it must never exceed `capacity`.

Because positions are at most 1000, a **difference array** of size 1001 gives O(n + 1000) without sorting.
complexity: O(n log n) with sorting, O(n + K) with a difference array · O(n) space
followups: Return the busiest stretch of road.
Meeting Rooms II (#253) is the same sweep.
Multiple cars — minimum number needed.

title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
statement:
`s` contains `'('`, `')'` and lowercase letters. Remove the **minimum number** of parentheses so that the result is a valid parentheses string, and return it.

A string is valid if every `')'` closes an earlier unmatched `'('` and nothing is left open. Letters are ignored for validity. Any valid result with the minimum number of removals is accepted.
constraints: s[i] is '(', ')' or a lowercase letter.

examples.explanation: "lee(t(co)de)" and "lee(t(c)ode)" are also accepted.

gens.name: Long string (n = 100,000)
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return ["".join(rng.choice("(()a)") for _ in range(100000))]

hints: A ')' is invalid if there is no unmatched '(' before it.
Push the index of each '(' on a stack; a ')' pops one or is marked for removal.
Whatever indices are left on the stack at the end are unmatched '(' — remove them too.
approach:
**Stack of indices.** Scan left to right. Push the index of every `'('`. A `')'` pops a match, or is marked for deletion if the stack is empty. After the scan, the indices still on the stack are unmatched `'('` — delete them. Every deletion was forced, so the count is minimal.

O(1)-extra-space variant: a left-to-right pass drops unmatched `')'`, then a right-to-left pass drops the excess `'('`.
complexity: O(n) time · O(n) space
followups: Do it without a stack (two passes with counters).
Return all valid strings with the minimum number of removals (#301, BFS / backtracking).
Only return how many removals are needed (#921).

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree III
statement:
Every node has a `parent` pointer (the root's parent is `None`). Given **only two nodes** `p` and `q` — not the root — return their lowest common ancestor.

In the tests the whole tree is written as a level-order list (first line) so you can see it; your method receives only `p` and `q`, and the judge reads `.val` from the node you return.
constraints: p ≠ q, and both are in the tree.
reference:
class Solution:
    def lowestCommonAncestor(self, p, q):
        a, b = p, q
        while a is not b:                 # each walks its own path then the other's: lengths equalise
            a = a.parent if a else q
            b = b.parent if b else p
        return a

gens.name: Tree with 100,000 nodes
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    t = rand_tree(rng, 100000, -10**6, 10**6)
    v = tree_values(t)
    return [t, v[-1], v[-2]]

hints: With parent pointers this is the 'intersection of two linked lists' problem.
A set of p's ancestors works in O(h) time and O(h) space.
For O(1) space: walk two pointers up; when one reaches None, restart it at the other node. They meet at the LCA.
approach: Each node's ancestor chain is a linked list ending at the root, so the LCA is where the two lists **intersect**. Walk pointer `a` from `p` and `b` from `q`; when a pointer falls off the root, restart it at the *other* start node. After at most `depth(p) + depth(q)` steps both have walked the same total distance and meet at the intersection.
complexity: O(h) time · O(1) space
followups: Without parent pointers (#236).
LCA of many nodes (#1676).
Answer many LCA queries quickly (binary lifting).

title: Buildings With an Ocean View
pattern: Scan from the right with a running maximum
statement:
`heights[i]` is the height of building `i` in a row. The ocean is to the **right** of the last building. A building has an ocean view if **every** building to its right is strictly shorter.

Return the indices of buildings with an ocean view, in increasing order.

examples.explanation: Building 1 is blocked by building 2 (height 3).

gens.name: Large input, all buildings visible
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [list(range(100000, 0, -1))]

hints: Whether building i can see the ocean depends only on the tallest building to its right.
Scan from right to left keeping the maximum height seen so far.
Collect indices on the way and reverse at the end (or use a monotonic stack from the left).
approach:
Scan **right to left** with `tallest`, the maximum height seen so far. Building `i` has a view exactly when `heights[i] > tallest`. Reverse the collected indices to get increasing order.

Scanning left to right with a monotonic decreasing stack also works: each new building pops every shorter-or-equal building it blocks.
complexity: O(n) time · O(1) extra space (output excluded)
followups: The ocean is on the left instead.
Ocean on both sides — return buildings that see either.
Heights arrive as a stream from left to right; maintain the answer online (monotonic stack).

title: Detect Squares
statement:
Points are added to the plane one at a time (duplicates allowed). For a query point, count the ways to choose **three stored points** that form an **axis-aligned square with positive area** together with the query point.

* `DetectSquares()` creates an empty structure.
* `add(point)` adds `[x, y]`.
* `count(point)` returns the number of such squares.

examples.explanation: After [11,2] is added twice, two squares share the same corners.

hints: Store how many times each point was added.
Fix the query point; a square is determined by its diagonal corner (px, py) with |px − x| = |py − y| ≠ 0.
Multiply the counts of the three other corners — duplicates multiply.
approach: Keep a counter of points. For `count(x, y)`, iterate over stored points `(px, py)` that could be the **opposite diagonal corner** (`|px − x| == |py − y| > 0`); the other corners are then fixed at `(px, y)` and `(x, py)`. Add the product of the three counts.
complexity: O(1) add · O(P) count (P distinct points) · O(P) space
followups: Only iterate points sharing the query's x column — keep a per-column index.
Count rectangles instead of squares.
Squares need not be axis-aligned.

title: Stock Price Fluctuation
statement:
Records of a stock's price arrive **out of order**, and a record may **correct** an earlier price for the same timestamp.

* `StockPrice()` creates an empty tracker.
* `update(timestamp, price)` sets the price at `timestamp` (overwriting any earlier value for that timestamp).
* `current()` returns the price at the **latest** timestamp seen.
* `maximum()` / `minimum()` return the highest / lowest price over all **current** records.

`current`, `maximum` and `minimum` are only called after at least one update.

examples.explanation: update(1, 3) corrects the price at time 1, so the maximum drops from 10 to 5.

gens.name: 100,000 operations

hints: A hash map timestamp → price handles corrections and current().
Scanning all prices for max / min is O(n) per call — too slow for 10⁵ calls.
Push every (price, timestamp) into a max-heap and a min-heap; when the top no longer matches the map, it is stale — pop it (lazy deletion).
approach:
Map `timestamp → price`, plus the latest timestamp for `current()`. For `maximum()` / `minimum()` keep a max-heap and a min-heap of `(price, timestamp)` pairs. Corrections are not removed eagerly: when the top of a heap disagrees with the map, it is **stale**, so pop it and look again. Each pushed entry is popped at most once.

A sorted container (balanced BST / `SortedList`) keyed on price with counts is the other standard answer.
complexity: O(log n) amortised per operation · O(n) space
followups: Also report the average price.
Maximum over the last T seconds only.
Implement it with a balanced BST / sorted map instead of heaps.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
statement: You are given `k` linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge them into one sorted linked list and return it.
starter:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: List[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        pass

gens.name: 1,000 lists of 10 nodes
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [[sorted(rng.randint(-10000, 10000) for _ in range(10)) for _ in range(1000)]]

hints: Merging lists one after another re-walks the growing result k times: O(k · N).
At every step the next node is the smallest current head — a min-heap finds it in O(log k).
Python cannot compare ListNode objects: push (val, index, node) so ties are broken by index.
approach:
Put the head of each list in a **min-heap** keyed by value. Repeatedly pop the smallest node, append it to the result, and push its successor. Each of the N nodes passes through a heap of size ≤ k.

**Divide and conquer** (merge lists in pairs, halving k each round) also gives O(N log k) without a heap.
complexity: O(N log k) time · O(k) space
followups: Merge k sorted arrays — and the k-way merge step of external sorting.
Find the k-th smallest element across k sorted lists.
Smallest range covering an element from each of k lists (#632).

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: `height[i]` is the height of a bar of width 1. After it rains, how many units of water are trapped between the bars?

gens.name: Large input (n = 20,000)
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [[rng.randint(0, 100000) for _ in range(20000)]]

hints: Water above bar i = min(highest bar to its left, highest bar to its right) − height[i].
Precomputing left-max and right-max arrays gives O(n) time and O(n) space.
With two pointers, the side with the smaller current bar is bounded by its own running max — process that side.
approach:
Water above `i` is `min(maxLeft, maxRight) − height[i]`.

**Two pointers.** Keep `lmax` and `rmax`. If `height[l] < height[r]`, the right side already has a bar at least as tall as anything that limits `l`, so the water at `l` is decided by `lmax` alone: add `lmax − height[l]` and move `l`. Symmetrically for the right.
complexity: O(n) time · O(1) space
followups: Trapping Rain Water II: a 2D elevation map (#407, heap + BFS).
Bars arrive one at a time — can you update the answer incrementally?
Solve it with a monotonic stack.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement:
Given strings `s` and `t`, return the **shortest substring of `s`** that contains every character of `t`, including duplicates. If no such substring exists, return `""`.

If several windows share the minimum length, any of them is accepted.
constraints: s and t consist of English letters.

examples.explanation: t needs two 'a's; s has one.

gens.name: Long string
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    s = "".join(rng.choice("ABCDEFGHIJ") for _ in range(100000))
    t = "".join(rng.choice("ABCDEFGHIJ") for _ in range(40))
    return [s, t]

hints: Expand the right edge until the window covers t; then shrink the left edge as far as possible.
Track how many required characters are still missing, so 'is the window valid?' is O(1).
A count map that goes negative means the window has surplus of that character — safe to drop from the left.
approach:
**Expand / contract sliding window.** `need[c]` counts how many more of `c` the window requires; `missing` is the total still required.

* Move `right`: decrement `need[s[right]]`; if it was positive, one fewer character is missing.
* When `missing == 0` the window is valid: advance `left` past surplus characters (`need < 0`), record the window, then give up `s[left]` to look for a shorter one.

Every index is added once and removed once.
complexity: O(|s| + |t|) time · O(alphabet) space
followups: Return the shortest window containing t as a subsequence (#727).
s is a huge stream and t is small — what can you keep in memory?
Find all windows of the minimum length.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
pattern: Postorder gain with clipping at zero
statement:
A **path** is a sequence of nodes where consecutive nodes are connected by an edge; each node appears at most once and the path need not pass through the root. A path contains at least one node.

Return the maximum sum of node values over all paths.
starter:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def maxPathSum(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        pass

gens.name: Tree with 30,000 nodes
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [rand_tree(rng, 30000, -1000, 1000, distinct=False)]

hints: Every path has a single highest node where it bends.
For each node, compute the best downward 'gain' starting there: val + max(left gain, right gain, 0).
The best path bending at node = val + max(left gain, 0) + max(right gain, 0). Track the global maximum.
approach:
Postorder. `gain(n)` = best sum of a path that **starts at n and goes down** one side: `n.val + max(gain(left), gain(right), 0)` — negative branches are clipped to 0. While computing it, the best path **bending at n** is `n.val + max(gainL, 0) + max(gainR, 0)`; keep the maximum over all nodes.

Initialise the answer to −∞, not 0: all values may be negative.
complexity: O(n) time · O(h) space
followups: Return the path itself.
Maximum path sum between two leaves.
Same question on a general tree / DAG.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement:
Design a structure that receives integers one at a time and can report the **median** of everything received so far. With an even count, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

* `MedianFinder()` creates the structure.
* `addNum(num)` adds an integer.
* `findMedian()` returns the median (answers within 10⁻⁵ are accepted).
constraints: findMedian is only called after at least one addNum.

gens.name: 50,000 operations

hints: Sorting on every findMedian is O(n log n) per query.
Split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half.
A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half expose both middle values at their roots. Keep sizes within one.
approach: **Two heaps**: `lo` (max-heap) holds the smaller half and `hi` (min-heap) the larger half, with `len(lo)` equal to `len(hi)` or one more. To add, push into `lo`, move `lo`'s maximum to `hi` (so every low ≤ every high), and move one back if `hi` grew larger. The median is `lo`'s root, or the mean of both roots.
complexity: O(log n) per addNum · O(1) per findMedian · O(n) space
followups: All numbers are in [0, 100] — O(1) with counting.
99% of numbers are in [0, 100].
Median of a sliding window (#480) — deletions are now needed.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
statement: From each cell you may move up, down, left or right, but only to a cell with a **strictly larger** value. Return the length (number of cells) of the longest increasing path in `matrix`.

gens.name: 200 × 200 matrix
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [[[rng.randint(0, 10**4) for _ in range(200)] for _ in range(200)]]

gens.name: Smooth 60 × 60 matrix (long paths)
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    return [[[r * 60 + c + rng.randint(0, 2) for c in range(60)] for r in range(60)]]

hints: Plain DFS from every cell re-explores the same paths: exponential.
The longest path starting at a cell never changes — memoise it.
'Strictly increasing' means the moves form a DAG, so there are no cycles to worry about.
approach: Because moves are strictly increasing, the cells form a **DAG**. Let `best(r, c)` be the longest path starting at `(r, c)`: `1 + max(best(neighbour))` over larger neighbours. Compute it with **DFS + memoisation**, or — as the reference does — iterate cells from largest value to smallest so each neighbour's answer is ready (a topological order).
complexity: O(R · C · log(R · C)) with sorting, O(R · C) with memoised DFS · O(R · C) space
followups: Return the path itself.
Allow moves to cells that are equal or larger (cycles appear — what changes?).
Diagonal moves allowed.

title: Swim in Rising Water
pattern: Minimax path: Dijkstra / binary search + BFS / Union-Find
statement:
`grid` is an `n × n` elevation map containing each value `0 … n² − 1` exactly once. At time `t` the water level is `t`, and you can swim between adjacent cells (4 directions) if **both** elevations are at most `t`. Swimming takes no time.

Return the minimum time at which you can reach the bottom-right cell starting from the top-left.
constraints: grid is a permutation of 0 … n² − 1

gens.name: 50 × 50 grid

hints: The time needed along a path is the maximum elevation on it; you want the path minimising that maximum.
Dijkstra works if a path's 'cost' is max(...) instead of a sum.
Alternative: binary search on t and check reachability with BFS — O(n² log n).
approach:
This is a **minimax path** problem: a path's cost is its largest elevation. Dijkstra still works with `cost = max(current, next elevation)` because that cost never decreases along a path. Pop the cell with the lowest cost; the first time the target is popped, its cost is the answer.

Equivalent: binary-search the time `t` with a BFS feasibility check, or add cells in increasing elevation into a Union-Find until the corners connect.
complexity: O(n² log n) time · O(n²) space
followups: Path With Minimum Effort (#1631) — cost is the largest height difference.
Return the actual path.
Elevations are not distinct — anything change?

title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination
statement:
`grid` contains `0` (empty) and `1` (obstacle). Moving up, down, left or right costs one step. You may **eliminate at most `k` obstacles** along the way.

Return the minimum number of steps from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, or `-1` if impossible. Both corners are empty.

gens.name: 40 × 40 grid, k = 20
gens.code:
def gen(rng):
    g = [[1 if rng.random() < 0.4 else 0 for _ in range(40)] for _ in range(40)]
    g[0][0] = g[39][39] = 0
    return [g, 20]

hints: Plain BFS finds shortest paths, but the state must include how many eliminations you have left.
BFS over (row, col, remaining) — at most R · C · (k + 1) states.
Prune: if you reach a cell with fewer eliminations left than a previous visit, it cannot do better.
approach:
**BFS on an expanded state** `(row, col, eliminations left)`. Stepping onto an obstacle costs one elimination. BFS explores by number of steps, so the first time the target is dequeued gives the answer.

Two prunings: if `k ≥ R + C − 2` you can walk the Manhattan path straight through; and keep, per cell, the most eliminations left on any visit so far — a later visit with fewer left is dominated.
complexity: O(R · C · k) time and space
followups: Each obstacle has a different removal cost (Dijkstra).
Minimise eliminations instead of steps (0-1 BFS, #2290).
Return the path.
